patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH] mm/mempolicy: apply bind policies against the scoped allocation zone

version_history.subject: [PATCH] mm/mempolicy: apply bind policies against the scoped allocation zone

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch addresses an issue where QEMU fails to start a guest with a VFIO device when the guest RAM comes from a memory backend bound to a movable-only node. The problem arises because the policy zone is not being checked against the current GFP context, leading to pin-scoped faults falling back onto the movable-only nodemask. To fix this, the patch modifies the `apply_policy_zone` function to check the policy zone against the current GFP context.

review_comments.author: Joshua Hahn
review_comments.summary: Identified the problem as a missing check of current_gfp_context in apply_policy_zone, which led to pin-scoped faults falling back onto the movable-only nodemask. Approved the patch and suggested that other places might be missing this check.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Sat, Oct 17, 2026 at 10:33 PM Gregory Price (Meta) <gourry@gourry.net> wrote:
>
> QEMU fails to start a guest with a VFIO device when guest RAM comes
> from a memory backend bound to a movable-only node:
>
>   vfio_container_dma_map(0x55b1b1317800, 0x0, 0x10000000,
>                          0x7f39a2200000)
>     = -12 (Cannot allocate memory)
>
> VFIO pins guest RAM when the device is realized, and the pin faults
> the pages in. io_uring fixed buffers fail the same way. Faulting the
> range in before pinning lets the same pin succeed, since resident
> pages are migrated off the node instead.
>
> A long-term pin faults under memalloc_pin_save(). PF_MEMALLOC_PIN makes
> current_gfp_context() clear __GFP_MOVABLE, but policy_nodemask() tests
> apply_policy_zone() against the caller's gfp.
>
> The bind keeps its movable-only nodemask, and the allocation finds no
> usable zone:
>
>   page allocation failure:
>       order:0,
>       mode:0x140dc2(GFP_HIGHUSER|__GFP_ZERO|__GFP_COMP),
>       nodemask=1,cpuset=/,mems_allowed=0-1
>
>   Call Trace:
>    warn_alloc+0x136/0x150
>    __alloc_frozen_pages_noprof+0xed8/0x1720
>    alloc_pages_mpol+0xaa/0x170
>    vma_alloc_folio_noprof+0x65/0xd0
>    __handle_mm_fault+0x137b/0x1ac0
>    handle_mm_fault+0xa0/0x270
>    __get_user_pages+0x250/0xfd0
>    __gup_longterm_locked+0x116/0x870
>    gup_fast_fallback+0xcfc/0xdf0
>    pin_user_pages_fast+0x47/0x60
>    io_pin_pages+0x9a/0x110
>
> Base page faults fail with -ENOMEM.
> hugetlb faults fail with -EFAULT.
>
> Check the policy zone against current_gfp_context(gfp), so a pin-scoped
> fault falls back off the movable-only nodemask, like any other
> non-movable allocation under the same bind.

Hi Gregory,

LGTM, thank you for making it so easy to review!
I wonder if other places are missing current_gfp_context as well.

Reviewed-by: Joshua Hahn <joshua.hahnjy@gmail.com>

> Tested in qemu with a dax/kmem movable-only node 1. io_uring and VFIO
> pins of unfaulted base pages and 2MB hugetlb pages now succeed and land
> on node 0 (correct). QEMU now starts with the same backend binding.
>
> Fixes: 8e3560d963d2 ("mm: honor PF_MEMALLOC_PIN for all movable pages")
> Cc: stable@vger.kernel.org
> Signed-off-by: Gregory Price (Meta) <gourry@gourry.net>
> ---
>  mm/mempolicy.c | 2 +-
>  1 file changed, 1 insertion(+), 1 deletion(-)
>
> diff --git a/mm/mempolicy.c b/mm/mempolicy.c
> index 70298fded1b4a..0884c629670dd 100644
> --- a/mm/mempolicy.c
> +++ b/mm/mempolicy.c
> @@ -2302,7 +2302,7 @@ static nodemask_t *policy_nodemask(gfp_t gfp, struct mempolicy *pol,
>                 break;
>         case MPOL_BIND:
>                 /* Restrict to nodemask (but not on lower zones) */
> -               if (apply_policy_zone(pol, gfp_zone(gfp)) &&
> +               if (apply_policy_zone(pol, gfp_zone(current_gfp_context(gfp))) &&
>                     cpuset_nodemask_valid_mems_allowed(&pol->nodes))
>                         nodemask = &pol->nodes;
>                 if (pol->home_node != NUMA_NO_NODE)
> --
> 2.53.0-Meta
>

patches_reviewed.subject: Re: [PATCH] nfsd: fix out-of-bounds read of sv_permsocks when starting a thread
patches_reviewed.patch_summary: This patch fixes an out-of-bounds read issue in the nfsd kernel module when starting a thread. The problem occurs because the code attempts to access the sv_permsocks field of the rqstp->rq_server structure without checking if it's valid. To fix this, the patch introduces a helper function that allows accessing the nfsd_net structure through the rqstp->rq_server->sv_stats field, avoiding the need for extra locking and socket lists.

[PATCH v3] kernfs: allocate inodes and dentry outside kernfs_rwsem

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch addresses long stalls in kernfs due to allocation of inodes and dentries while holding the kernfs_rwsem lock, which can lead to memory reclaim delays and OOM killer activations. The patch allocates inodes outside the lock and frees them if unused, similar to previous commits for other use cases. This change reduces wait times in various scenarios, including cgroupfs operations, and improves overall system performance.

review_comments.author: Jori Koolstra
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer Jori Koolstra noted that mentioning memcg is unnecessary and not relevant to understanding the patch, and complimented the author on implementing a similar solution in another series.

Reviewer Jori Koolstra expressed concern about the complexity of the kernfs_iop_lookup() function's contract, questioning whether an output parameter is truly necessary for such a simple function.

reviewer questioned the correctness of removing locking in kernfs_get_tree(), expressing uncertainty about potential serialization issues

Reviewer noted that the patch does not actually allocate inodes and dentry outside kernfs_rwsem as claimed, but instead only moves kernfs_get_parent_dentry() to hold the lock around inode lookup
review_comments.raw_body:
I wouldn't mention memcg here per se, it is not relevant to grasp its
use. In another series I have implemented almost the same thing (but you
did it better!).

---

I understand this is intended to have some kind of ownership semantics,
but I must say for such a simple function, I find the contract quite
complex to check. Do we really need an out parameter here?

---

What are you serializing against here? I've been looking at this as well
recently, and I thought we could just get rid of the locking here. But
on second look, I am not so sure what is correct.

Is there anything that serializes kernfs_get_tree() with root node
removal?

---

Thanks,
Jori.
